title: Given an array of numbers and a window size K, find the median of every contiguous window of size K as the window slides from left to right. Explain how two heaps with lazy deletion maintain the window median efficiently.
shortTitle: Sliding Window Median (Two Heaps with Lazy Deletion)
keyPoints: Max-heap for the smaller half, min-heap for the larger half, median sits at the boundary
Lazy deletion: record departing values in a count map, purge only when they surface at a heap top
Track logical balance separately because lazily deleted elements still occupy heap space
Prune both heap tops before reading the median so no stale value corrupts the answer
Each window slide costs O(log n) amortized time; total is O(n log n)
Use a count map (not a set) for the removal structure to handle duplicate values correctly

s1_definition.oneliner: Two heaps for the window, add the new element, lazily mark the old one, rebalance, and read the median at the boundary.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Sliding Window Median** – find the median of every contiguous window of size K as the window slides across an array.
- **Two heaps** – a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half; the median sits at their boundary.
- **Lazy deletion** – departing elements are recorded in a count map and physically removed from a heap only when they surface at the top.
- **Logical balance** – tracked separately from raw heap sizes because lazily deleted elements still take up space.
- **Complexity** – O(n log n) total time (O(log n) amortized per slide), O(n) space for the heaps and the removal map.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the risk team watches the median transaction amount over the last K transactions as a rolling risk indicator. As each new transaction arrives, the oldest drops out. Rajesh keeps two buckets: a low bucket (max-heap) and a high bucket (min-heap). Rather than hunting for the departing value inside a bucket, he notes it should be ignored and physically drops it only when it bubbles to the top.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Sliding Window Median extends the streaming-median two-heaps structure to a fixed window of size K. A max-heap holds the smaller half and a min-heap holds the larger half, with the median sitting at the boundary. The new difficulty is removing the element that ages out of the window, which a priority queue cannot do cheaply for arbitrary values.

Lazy deletion solves this: when an element departs the window, record it in a count map. Physically remove it from the heap only when it surfaces at the top during pruning. Each element is pruned at most once, keeping the amortized cost at O(log n) per slide. Because lazily deleted elements still occupy heap space, track logical heap sizes separately from raw sizes, and prune both tops before reading the median.

The count map (not a set) handles duplicates correctly. If the window contains two copies of the same value and only one departs, the count map decrements by one while a set would mark both as gone.

At the National Bank of India, the risk team monitors the rolling median of the last K transaction amounts. As each new transaction arrives, the oldest one ages out, and the median updates in O(log n) amortized time. The lazy deletion keeps the system responsive even with duplicate amounts and long sliding windows.

Remember one sentence: two heaps for the halves, lazy deletion for the departing element, logical sizes for balance, and prune the tops before reading the median.
